title: Commitment & Consistency
description: The drive to align your future actions with your past words, beliefs, and behaviors.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Once we make a choice or take a stand, we face personal and interpersonal pressures to behave consistently with that commitment. We hate looking like hypocrites.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Cognitive dissonance. When our actions contradict our stated beliefs or past choices, it causes mental stress. Our brain forces us to stay consistent to relieve that stress.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: Business: Free trial requiring deep configuration. Once you spend an hour setting it up, you stay.
Sales: Asking 'Do you care about your family's safety?' before pitching an alarm system.
Politics: Getting someone to wear a campaign pin makes them statistically more likely to vote.
Daily Life: Publicly posting a New Year's resolution on social media to force accountability.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Sales rep: 'Hi, do you consider yourself someone who cares about the environment?'
Customer: 'Yes, absolutely.'
Sales rep: 'Great! Then you'll want to donate $5 to our clean water initiative today.'
Customer: (Trapped by their own words) 'Uh, sure.'

sections.title: Pattern Recognition
content: Starting a conversation by getting you to agree to universally accepted truths ('Do you like saving money?').
Getting you to write something down or make a public statement.
Small, seemingly harmless initial requests that slowly escalate.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Encouraging positive habits, like having someone sign a public pledge to quit smoking or publicly sharing personal fitness goals.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Bait-and-switch tactics, low-balling (getting someone to agree to a cheap price, then adding hidden fees after they are mentally committed to the purchase).

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Questions that force you to confirm your identity ('Are you a smart investor?').
Requests to sign a non-binding 'statement of intent'.
Feeling trapped by something you said 5 minutes ago.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Realize that changing your mind is completely acceptable.
Ask yourself: 'Knowing what I know now, would I still make the same choice?'
Recognize the setup questions and refuse to answer them.
Tell them point blank: 'I see what you are doing, and I am not committing.'

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Sticking with a terrible investment or product simply because they already spent time on it (sunk cost fallacy).
Answering leading questions from salespeople out of politeness.

sections.title: Case Study
sections.content: A restaurant struggling with "no-shows" changed their receptionist's script from "Please call if you change your plans" to "Will you please call if you change your plans?" and waiting for the customer to say "Yes". Simply forcing that tiny verbal commitment dropped no-shows from 30% to 10%.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: 1. Humans have a desperate need to appear consistent.
2. Public and written commitments are the most powerful.
3. Beware of innocent 'setup' questions.
4. It is strictly okay to change your mind when new facts arrive.
